text: Good day, everyone. My name is Sandra E. Maynard. I am the Pro Vice-Chancellor of Global Affairs at the University of the West Indies and the President of the International School for Development Justice. It's my pleasure to speak here today around AI governance, a Caribbean regional imperative. Now, when we consider Caribbean AI governance, it is essential, not optional. When we consider that AI is reshaping the world economies through automation, data, analytics and intelligence system that enhance productivity across sectors. For the Caribbean, this transformation occurs within a unique context of being small island developing states with limited resources, high connectivity costs and economies heavily dependent on tourism, agriculture and services. Now, this is not to the exclusion of other small island developing states but the Caribbean region faces a real digital divide paradox.

text: An example is our project on inclusive hiring and digital skills development, which counted systemic unemployment and exclusion by demonstrating how AI can make hiring practices fairer and digital skills more accessible. Another example is the inaugural AI and data science boot camp, where we built AI literacy amongst underrepresented groups to help redress intersectional gender imbalances and broaden participation in digital economies. So these slides or these examples show that while AI systems can mirror and reinforce inequitable social and economic models, they also hold the potential to challenge them. text: Hello, my name is Deborah Berlin. I'm Executive Director of Project Goal, the project to get older adults online. I'm pleased to join you to talk about technology innovations, AI and aging. The world is aging. The number of older individuals globally is growing exponentially. According to the World Health Organization between the years 2015 and 2050, the proportion of the world's population of those 60 years and older will nearly double from 12% to 22%. In just five years, 2030, one in six people in the world will be 60 and older. As older populations increase and the working and younger aging ages decrease, resources to assist with aging need grow increasingly scarce, creating a significant gap in services.

text: For a young graduate entering the job market, AI's automation of tasks in sectors like data entry, customer service, and even basic coding is a genuine concern. It can feel like the goalposts are moving just as they are about to score. The risk isn't just job loss, it's a potential erosion of creative confidence. If AI can generate art, if it can generate music and essays in seconds, what is the value of human creativity? This can lead to a dependency where we stop exercising our own creative muscles, the very muscles that make us innovative and resilient. However, focusing on the risks is a disservice to our youth. The real conversation is about transition and not replacement.

text: The UNESCO information for all program working group on information accessibility is hosting its sixth online AI for IE conference on Sunday, September 28, 2025 to commemorate the international day for universal access to information. In addition to the main event on September 28, we are proud to have satellite event taking place worldwide. In India, America, Canada, South Africa, Zimbabwe, Europe, Chile and Latin America. Artificial intelligence is no longer a distant concept. It has rapidly evolved to become an integral part of our daily lives, influencing how we learn, create, communicate and access information. This conference explores how artificial intelligence can be harnessed to make information more inclusive, accessible and empowering for all. I am Samrithi Arora, a member of UNESCO, a FAPS working group on information accessibility and an advocate on record at Supreme Court of India.

text: Kia ora tato katoa. Thank you so much for the opportunity to join you today from Aotearoa, New Zealand, for the UNESCO AI for AI conference. The Christchurch Hall was born out of the unprecedented horror of the 2019 terrorist attacking Christchurch that killed 51 people and was livestreamed online. It was a wake-up call to the world. Today, the Christchurch Hall is a multi-stakeholder community of over 130 online platforms, governments and civil society organisations. With a clear mission to eliminate terrorist and violent extremist content online while upholding human rights and preserving a free, open and secure internet. Supporting this work is the Christchurch Hall Foundation, an independent, not-for-profit that I lead, that enables and strengthens the core community.

text: At its core, our work is about online safety within the broader context of internet governance and increasingly AI governance. In today's shifting geopolitical landscape, this mission is more urgent than ever. We began with a determination that the events of March 15, 2019 must never happen again. We remain active because online TVAC is not just a digital issue, it's a matter of national security, economic stability, public safety and the prevention of radicalisation, especially among the young. These are concerns shared across our diverse community and rightly so. Our work is guided by the 25 commitments of the Christchurch Hall, grouped into five key themes, all focused on eliminating terrorist and violent extremist content online. The themes are information integrity in TVAC, new technology in TVAC, gender-based violence and violent extremism, youth and radicalisation to violent extremism, offline linkages and TVAC.

text: Key concerns in our domain include the amplification of harmful content. Engagement-based algorithms can unintentionally promote terrorist and violent extremist material. Bias and discrimination remain an issue. AI may reflect or reinforce societal biases, disproportionately impacting marginalized communities. Transparency remains a concern. Many models operate as black boxes, making decisions difficult to interpret or to challenge. And security vulnerabilities are a concern too. AI can be weaponised as bread disinformation, deep fakes or rather malicious content. To address these risks, we advocate for explainable AI systems in moderation and recommendation, for independent audits and impact assessments of platform AI tools. For frameworks that embed human rights, fairness and inclusion in AI design, for multi-state colder collaboration to shape ethical standards and policy development.

The 6th Global Conference will take place on the 28th of September on Get The Town platform, and we kindly invite you to register for the event, to get acquainted with presentations of over 70 speakers, participate in live interactive sessions, and in the informal network. Does generative AI have to be treated as a mere information intermediary or as a content creator in its own right? This is a very, very important question for regulation as well. To the extent that we say generative AI is a content creator, the providers of such systems, such as a Google for example, there would be fully liable for the content that their AI systems create. But to the extent that we say no, no, they are mere intermediaries, they essentially merely summarize and convey what others have said before

fragment_id: 0094_otyBopReCRs_Jan Christopher Kalbhenn - AI ⧸ Information Access： Importance of media law_0001
source_video: 0094_otyBopReCRs_Jan Christopher Kalbhenn - AI ⧸ Information Access： Importance of media law
text: This speech is on the importance of media law in the field of AI and information access. When we talk about how artificial intelligence is changing the way we access information, the media law plays the central role. Media such as the press and broadcasters provide us with information we need to make informed decision, for example, in elections or emergencies, but also in everyday life. But the media landscape is facing major challenges today. Traditional media companies are facing a significant reduction in their reach and presence across Europe, particularly in rural areas. At the same time, the digital transformation has radically changed the way information is produced, distributed and consumed. New dependencies on large technology companies or algorithm driven platforms are also emerging.

text: One of the biggest dangers is the increasing dependence on large AI providers and technology companies. These companies control the algorithms and technologies used in media companies. This allows them to dictate their terms and influence the way information is disseminated. This concentration of power with a few providers carries the risk that media companies had less control over their own content and work processes and become dependent on the business models and decisions of AI providers. Another risk lies in the possibility of blurring the line between human journalism and AI generated content. If readers and viewers can no longer distinguish whether an article or contribution was created by a human or an AI, there is a risk of loss of trust in the media.

text: Hello, my name is Jan Oster, and I'm a professor of media law and digital law at the University of Osnabrück in Germany. And I would like to share my thoughts on artificial intelligence and diversity of opinion. What is diversity of opinion? In essence, the concept of diversity of opinion, we can also speak of plurality or pluralism of opinion, requires the guarantee of the widest possible circulation of news, ideas and opinions, as well as the widest access to information by society as a whole. In the European Union, we might be even more familiar with the concept of media pluralism, which is even codified in the U Charter of Fundamental Rights, media pluralism or media plurality

text: Greetings, everyone I am Dr. Mukesh Mera from New Delhi India, it is an honor to be here today at the fifth Artificial Intelligence for Information Conference. I would like to extend my gratitude to the Organizing Committee for giving me this opportunity to discuss the profound role of AI playing in medicine. As a senior director at Mac Super Special Hospital Delhi, with over 36 years of medical practice, I have witnessed first hand the transformative impact of technology on healthcare, holding fellowships from Royal College of London, Glasgow and Edinburgh and American College of Physicians serving as an international examiner for MRCP UK Paces. I can truly appreciate the advancement that AI has brought to the field of medicine.

text: Hello, everyone. My name is Selen Cruz-Odixson. I am a business analyst who works in policy and governance development in the inclusion space with a keen interest in AI at ATV Financial. text: It has become customary to hear stories on how AI has wronged X group or community. We heard it with artists whose work was stolen for datasets in image generation with facial recognition software that couldn't distinguish between two different individuals of Asian descent and with hiring systems that actively discriminated against women. These are not one-off events nor are they isolated. They tell us something about our societies, how inclusion and existence on equitable terms is lacking and furthermore being exacerbated by AI. Of course, there are good stories too. AI being used to help in cancer research, accessibility tech, and learning as well. However, those harmful stories still persist. And the question arises, how do we use AI to help us on this journey of inclusion? We can't ignore the back end work of developing AI.

text: Journalism has traditionally been the backbone of democracy, guiding public understanding of complex issues through investigation and ethical reporting. But the rise of AI in journalism paired with platform driven news distribution is fragmenting this shared reality. Digital platforms now curate content based on engagement metrics. Likes, shares, clicks, rather than truthfulness or public interest. This shift has contributed to what many scholars refer to as an epistemic crisis in journalism. And the heart of this crisis is the blurring of lines between facts and fiction. AI often prioritizes sensationalism to maximize engagement and amplify misleading or force information at the expense of reliable reporting. This undermines journalism's credibility and erodes public trust, which are both crucial for a healthy democracy.

Technologies such as machine learning and AI have become integral to our daily activities enhancing accessibility in various ways. For example, screen readers and text-to-speech. AI-driven tools help us to access digital content more easily. As for navigation systems, they are AI-powered apps and canes, even a robotic AI guide dog to assist with orientation and mobility. This AI guide dog will be available to consumers quite soon too. These AI tools provide spoken directions, making it easier for a blind or visually impaired person to move to different environments. Then we have facial and object recognition. With the use of my iPhone camera, AI helps me to identify people and objects and this enhances my interaction with the world.

text: We identify three main ways that deepfakes can cause harm, those that demean, defraud and disinform. Deepfakes that defraud are used to deceive a target by misrepresenting someone else's identity. They are primarily used to assist fraudulent behaviour such as scam communications and false advertising. text: Welcome to the fourth Artificial Intelligence for Information Accessibility Conference. My name is Shamir Ahmed, I'm the Executive Director and founder of the Data Economy Policy Hub, the Deb Hub. Deb Hub is the first independent think tank that is founded by an Indigenous African woman in South Africa. Today, I will discuss with you responsible AI governance, structural inequalities and sustainability in the global solve. My discussion will be broken down into three parts. I will start with exploring the nexus of responsible AI, data governance and the environment. Second part, I will delve into what do intersectional inequality have to do with right data governance and the environment. In the last part, I will discuss some suggestions and what we can do about issues at the nexus of responsible AI, data governance and the environment.

text: Thank you for inviting me to speak at the 4th AI4IA conference. I will be talking about AI and technological sovereignty, specifically the appearance of new types of sovereignty as a result of the massive use of AI after COVID-19. This era is accompanied by an evolution on many levels, evolution of notions, new practices, and new phenomena. Thus, we see the appearance of auspheres of authority and new forms of non-state, political constitutions, where big tech becomes more powerful than the state. This explains the competition between these two actors and their race to technological sovereignty. COVID-19 is like a Westphalian system, a remarkable step in history. It is accelerating the transition to a society based on the massive use of AI and the appearance of new notions such as digital sovereignty, cyberspace sovereignty, and technological sovereignty.

text: So just to give you a basic overview of the project itself in 2021, June, my team applied for a grant through GP to study social justice implications of globally ramifying data vacation. The project advancing data justice research and practice aimed to widen the lens of current thinking around data justice and to provide actionable resources to help policymakers practitioners and impacted communities gain a broader understanding of what equitable freedom promoting and rights sustaining data collection governance and use should look like in an increasingly dynamic and global data innovation ecosystem. So when we engage the project initially, we had committed to carrying out an integrated literature view and annotated bibliography, a repository of use cases that demonstrated the ways in which civil society organizations were actually carrying out activities and practices of data justice.

text: Hello everyone, and thank you for inviting me. My name is Ivana Stepanovich. I am from the Institute of Advanced Studies in Kosek, Hungary. I would like to start by saying that AI-powered digital technologies have already paved the way to the rise of machine-agency. Now, what do I mean by that? I mean that we are increasingly relying on artificial intelligence and algorithmic systems, so to say, powered by AI, to delegate decision-making to algorithms. And this also means crucial decisions, such as ethical decisions. This is present across all human activities, all types of human activities, not all activities. And as we are increasingly using AI for very important tasks that were always traditionally being human, we need to ask what is the role of education of humans in the era of machine learning.

text: Ladies and gentlemen, good morning, good afternoon, good evening, wherever you are. My presentation raises questions about the future of human agency in the face of rapid incursion by machines and technology in all aspects of everyday life, including AI with the potential to become autonomous moral agents. Mankind has always been dependent on information, and it could be argued that we are information beings with everything about us coded in genes. So the quality of being human might be for some people no more than complex coding. This thinking comports with transhumanist philosophy which aspires to a redesign of humanity to allow us to transcend our biological limitations and to shape the human species through the direct application of technology.

text: As Nita Farani observes, there are no legal protections from having our mind involuntarily read. The law contemplates externalities in the sense that we should not be constrained from formulating thoughts and expressing them freely. But jurisprudence of the mind is about something else. It protects the brain as an operating system which should be invalid to intrusion by means of neural computation, meaning that third parties should not access a person's mental information or make inferences from their mental data whether it be neurological, cognitive, or effective information or collect any such data without the consent of the data subject. Third, the law should impose fiduciary responsibilities on technology companies as a response to information, asymmetry, and power imbalance between big tech governments and ordinary people.

text: Here, in this paper and in this short lecture, we will completely sidestep the conceptual philosophical issue of defining or measuring intelligence, as well as the practical question of whether a machine can be built to replace or mimic a person in the performance of even a specific task. Instead, we look more broadly at the concept that we term the human or machine issue, the H or M issue. In a future world, when in some interactions, machines will be able to mimic humans impressively, new social, psychological, functional and obviously technical issues are bound to become relevant. So here are some of the questions that come to mind immediately and in this paper, we actually discuss them. For example, will humans care about whether the agent they are interacting with is a human or a machine, and if yes, then why would they care?

text: Hello, my name is Danielle Davis and I am the tech and telecom policy council for the multicultural media and telecom Internet council more commonly known as MMTC. I would like to thank the information for all working group on information accessibility for their invitation to present on AI policy and ethics. In my presentation, I will discuss AI and its role in society and the legal and ethical implications it presents to black and other marginalized communities. Because at the end of the day, today, AI is everywhere in society. Sometimes it's fairly obvious and other times it's hidden under the covers. It can help us request rides. It can help us make our online purchases possible. It determines what you see on your social media feed and what movies and shows your streaming app recommends for you.

text: When that little wireless speaker in your living room acts on your request to turn on your favorite song, there's AI working to understand your speech so it can then determine what you want to accomplish and then carry out those instructions. However, there's an argument to be made regarding how much AI should be deployed in our daily lives because in many instances, AI can present many ethical concerns with these concerns disproportionately impacting black and other marginalized communities. So for purposes of this presentation, let's think of these ethical concerns in three different buckets. So we have the privacy and surveillance bucket, we have the bias and discrimination bucket, and then we have the bucket of role, the role of human judgment.

Son muchos los retos que tenemos los reguladores y especialmente en un mundo interconectado y con cambios en las conductes de los consumidores. No solo de las perspectivas de visual, sino en centorno de vida.
